notes.title: IAM: least privilege with roles, not keys
notes.gist: Give people and workloads temporary credentials through roles, grant only what they need, and lock the root user away.
points: Root user: turn on MFA, delete its access keys, and use it only for the few root-only tasks.
Roles hand out temporary STS credentials: instance profiles for EC2, execution roles for Lambda and ECS tasks.
Identity policies attach to users, groups and roles; resource policies such as S3 bucket policies name a Principal.
Cross-account access: a role in account B trusts account A, and users in A call sts:AssumeRole.
An explicit Deny always wins; with no Allow anywhere, the request is implicitly denied.
Federate a corporate directory through IAM Identity Center or SAML 2.0 instead of creating IAM users.
notes.tip: Access keys stored on an instance, in code or in an environment file are always the wrong answer. Pick an IAM role, which delivers rotating temporary credentials.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  APP[App on EC2] --> IP[Instance profile]
  IP --> STS[STS temporary credentials]
  STS --> R[IAM role policy]
  R -->|Allow| S3[(S3 bucket)]
  BP[Bucket policy] --> S3

notes.title: Multi-account guardrails: Organizations, SCPs, Control Tower
notes.gist: Split workloads into accounts, then cap what any account can do with SCPs on organizational units.
points: AWS Organizations groups accounts into OUs and gives consolidated billing with pooled volume discounts.
SCPs set the maximum permissions for accounts in an OU; they never grant anything on their own.
SCPs apply to every user and role in member accounts, including the member root user, but not to the management account.
Control Tower builds a landing zone with guardrails, a log archive account and an audit account.
IAM Identity Center gives one sign-in and permission sets across all accounts.
Resource Access Manager shares subnets, Transit Gateways and other resources between accounts.
notes.tip: Stop every account from doing X, even its administrators: an SCP on the OU. An IAM policy cannot restrict an account's own admins.

  OU1 --> A2[Account B]
  IDC[IAM Identity Center] --> A1
  IDC --> A2

notes.title: VPC security: subnets, security groups, NACLs, endpoints
notes.gist: Put only the load balancer in public subnets, keep app and data tiers private, and filter traffic in two layers.
points: A public subnet routes to an internet gateway; private subnets reach out through a NAT gateway in a public subnet.
Security groups are stateful, work per ENI, allow rules only, and can reference other security groups.
Network ACLs are stateless, work per subnet, have numbered allow and deny rules, and need return ephemeral ports open.
Blocking a specific bad IP range needs a NACL deny rule or WAF; security groups cannot deny.
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, and interface endpoints through PrivateLink for other services, keep traffic off the internet.
Site-to-Site VPN is encrypted over the internet; Direct Connect is private but not encrypted unless you add MACsec or a VPN.
notes.tip: Private instances that must reach S3 with no internet path: an S3 gateway endpoint, not a NAT gateway or a public IP.

flowchart LR
  IGW[Internet gateway] --> PUB[Public subnet: ALB and NAT GW]
  PUB --> PRIV[Private subnet: app tier SG]
  PRIV --> DB[(DB subnet: SG allows app SG only)]
  PRIV --> GWE[S3 gateway endpoint]
  GWE --> S3[(S3)]
  NACL[NACL: stateless subnet filter] -.-> PRIV

notes.title: Protecting applications: WAF, Shield, Cognito, Secrets Manager
notes.gist: Filter attacks at the edge, sign users in with a managed service, and never hard-code a secret.
points: WAF filters layer 7 traffic on CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway and AppSync: SQL injection, XSS, rate-based rules, geo match.
Shield Standard is free layer 3 and 4 DDoS protection; Shield Advanced adds the response team and DDoS cost protection.
Cognito user pools sign users in and issue tokens; identity pools swap tokens for temporary AWS credentials.
Secrets Manager stores and rotates database credentials automatically; Parameter Store is cheaper for plain config.
GuardDuty detects threats from logs, Macie finds personal data in S3, Inspector scans for vulnerabilities.
notes.tip: SQL injection or bad bots: WAF. DDoS with cost protection and a 24/7 response team: Shield Advanced. Rotating DB passwords: Secrets Manager.

notes.title: Data protection: KMS, TLS, retention and backups
notes.gist: Encrypt at rest with KMS, in transit with TLS, and enforce retention so data can be recovered.
points: Envelope encryption: a KMS key encrypts data keys, and the data keys encrypt the data.
Customer managed keys give you the key policy, rotation control and CloudTrail audit of every use.
S3 encryption: SSE-S3 is the default, SSE-KMS adds audit and key control, SSE-C means you supply the key.
An unencrypted RDS instance cannot be encrypted in place: snapshot, copy the snapshot encrypted, restore.
ACM issues free public TLS certificates for ALB, CloudFront and API Gateway and renews them.
S3 Object Lock enforces WORM retention; AWS Backup centralizes backup plans and cross-Region copies.
notes.tip: Audit who used the key and when: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key. Keys must sit in single-tenant hardware you control: CloudHSM.

flowchart LR
  APP[App] -->|GenerateDataKey| KMS[KMS key]
  KMS --> DK[Plaintext and encrypted data key]
  DK --> ENC[Encrypt data locally]
  ENC --> S3[(S3: ciphertext and encrypted key)]
  KMS --> CT[CloudTrail audit]

summary.tests: Who can do what across accounts, how traffic is filtered in and around a VPC, and how data is encrypted, retained and recovered.
must_know: Roles and STS temporary credentials beat long-lived access keys every time.
Explicit Deny wins; SCPs cap permissions but never grant them.
Security groups are stateful and allow-only; NACLs are stateless with allow and deny.
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free and keep traffic private.
WAF for layer 7 attacks, Shield for DDoS, GuardDuty for threats, Macie for PII.
SSE-KMS gives audit and key control; ACM gives free TLS certificates.
Secrets Manager rotates credentials; Parameter Store holds config cheaply.
traps: Putting access keys on EC2 or in code instead of attaching an IAM role.
Trying to block an IP with a security group; only a NACL or WAF can deny.
Thinking an SCP grants permissions or restricts the management account.

cards.q: An app on EC2 needs to read S3. What is the most secure way to give it credentials?
cards.a: Attach an IAM role through an instance profile. It supplies rotating temporary STS credentials; never store access keys on the instance.

cards.q: One policy allows an action and another explicitly denies it. Which wins?
cards.a: The explicit Deny. An explicit deny beats any allow, and with no allow at all the default is an implicit deny.

cards.q: Every account in an OU must be blocked from Regions outside the EU, even for admins. What do you use?
cards.a: A service control policy on the OU that denies actions outside the allowed Regions.

cards.q: Do SCPs grant permissions?
cards.a: No. They set the maximum available permissions; IAM policies in the account must still allow the action. SCPs do not apply to the management account.

cards.q: Users in account A must manage resources in account B. What is the standard pattern?
cards.a: A role in account B whose trust policy trusts account A. Users in A call sts:AssumeRole to switch into it.

cards.q: Staff should sign in once with corporate credentials to many AWS accounts. Which service?
cards.a: IAM Identity Center, federated with the corporate IdP or Active Directory, with permission sets per account.

cards.q: Security group or network ACL: which is stateless and supports deny rules?
cards.a: The network ACL. It works at the subnet level, evaluates numbered rules in order, and needs return ephemeral ports opened.

cards.q: How do you let only the app tier reach the database tier?
cards.a: Add an inbound rule on the database security group for the DB port, with the app tier's security group as the source.

cards.q: Private-subnet instances must reach S3 with no internet path and no extra data charge. What do you add?
cards.a: An S3 gateway VPC endpoint plus its route table entry. Gateway endpoints have no hourly or per-GB charge.

cards.q: Which service blocks SQL injection and rate-limits abusive IPs in front of an ALB?
cards.a: AWS WAF with managed rule groups and a rate-based rule, attached to the ALB or to CloudFront.

cards.q: What does Shield Advanced add over Shield Standard?
cards.a: The Shield Response Team, DDoS cost protection, layer 7 protection with WAF and advanced metrics. Standard is free layer 3 and 4 protection.

cards.q: Database passwords must rotate automatically every 30 days. Which service?
cards.a: AWS Secrets Manager, which has built-in rotation for RDS, Aurora, Redshift and DocumentDB.

cards.q: Which service finds personal data such as credit card numbers in S3 buckets?
cards.a: Amazon Macie. GuardDuty detects threats from logs; Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities.

cards.q: How do you encrypt an existing unencrypted RDS database?
cards.a: Snapshot it, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled using a KMS key, then restore a new instance from the encrypted copy.

cards.q: S3 data must use a key whose every use is logged in CloudTrail. Which encryption option?
cards.a: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key. With SSE-S3 you never see or control the key.

cards.q: Objects must be impossible to delete or overwrite for seven years, even by root. What do you enable?
cards.a: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a seven-year retention period. Governance mode can be bypassed with special permissions.

cards.q: Mobile app users need temporary AWS credentials to upload to their own S3 prefix. Which Cognito feature?
cards.a: A Cognito identity pool, which exchanges a user pool or social login token for temporary IAM role credentials.

notes.title: High availability in a Region: Multi-AZ everything
notes.gist: Survive the loss of an instance or a whole AZ by running every tier in at least two AZs.
points: Run an Auto Scaling group across two or more AZs behind an ALB with health checks.
RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ and fails the endpoint over automatically.
Read replicas are asynchronous and scale reads; they can be promoted, but that is not automatic failover.
Aurora keeps six copies across three AZs and usually fails over to a replica within about 30 seconds.
RDS Proxy pools connections, absorbs Lambda connection storms and shortens failover time.
S3 and EFS Standard are Regional and span AZs; an EBS volume lives in a single AZ.
notes.tip: High availability means Multi-AZ. Read performance means read replicas. A question that asks for both wants both.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  ALB[ALB] --> A[Instances in AZ a]
  ALB --> B[Instances in AZ b]
  A --> P[(RDS primary AZ a)]
  B --> P
  P -->|sync| S[(Standby AZ b)]
  P -->|async| RR[(Read replica)]

notes.title: Decoupling with SQS, SNS and EventBridge
notes.gist: Put a queue or an event bus between components so one can slow down or fail without losing work.
points: SQS buffers work between producers and consumers; scale the consumers on queue depth.
Standard queues: nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once, best-effort order. FIFO: strict order, exactly-once processing.
The visibility timeout hides a message while it is processed; set it longer than the processing time.
A dead-letter queue catches messages that fail more than maxReceiveCount times.
SNS pushes one message to many subscribers; SNS into several SQS queues is the fan-out pattern.
EventBridge routes events by content rules to many targets, including SaaS partners and other accounts.
notes.tip: Orders lost when the backend is slow or down: put SQS between the tiers. One event, many independent consumers: SNS fan-out or EventBridge.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  P[Producer] --> SNS[SNS topic]
  SNS --> Q1[[SQS queue A]]
  SNS --> Q2[[SQS queue B]]
  Q1 --> W1[Worker ASG]
  Q2 --> W2[Lambda]
  Q1 -.-> DLQ[[Dead-letter queue]]

notes.title: Disaster recovery: RPO, RTO and the four strategies
notes.gist: Pick the cheapest DR strategy whose recovery time and data loss meet the stated targets.
points: RPO is how much data you can afford to lose; RTO is how long you can afford to be down.
Backup and restore: cheapest, RPO and RTO measured in hours.
Pilot light: data replicated live, core services off until needed; recovery in tens of minutes.
Warm standby: a scaled-down but fully working copy always running; recovery in minutes.
Multi-site active-active: full capacity in two Regions; near-zero RTO and the highest cost.
Raise service quotas in the DR Region ahead of time so failover can actually scale.
notes.tip: Read the RTO and RPO first, then choose the cheapest strategy that meets them. Lowest cost with hours of downtime allowed is backup and restore.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  BR[Backup and restore: hours] --> PL[Pilot light: tens of minutes]
  PL --> WS[Warm standby: minutes]
  WS --> AA[Active-active: near zero]
  COST[Cost and RTO trade-off] -.-> AA

notes.title: Route 53 and cross-Region failover
notes.gist: DNS health checks steer users to a healthy Region, and the data layer replicates so that Region has the data.
points: Failover routing sends traffic to the secondary record when the primary health check fails.
Latency routing picks the lowest-latency Region; geolocation routes by user location; weighted splits by percentage.
Alias records point the zone apex at AWS resources and are free to query; a CNAME cannot sit at the apex.
Aurora Global Database and DynamoDB global tables replicate across Regions with about a second of lag.
S3 Cross-Region Replication copies new objects to another Region; enable versioning on both buckets.
notes.tip: Users must be served from their own country for legal reasons: geolocation, not latency routing.

flowchart LR

  R53 -->|healthy| P[Primary Region ALB]
  R53 -.->|health check fails| S[DR Region ALB]
  P --> AG[(Aurora Global primary)]
  AG -->|about 1s lag| AS[(Secondary Region cluster)]
  S --> AS

notes.title: Scalable, stateless, loosely coupled design
notes.gist: Keep compute stateless and scale it out, and let managed services orchestrate the steps.
points: Store sessions in ElastiCache or DynamoDB so any instance can serve any request.
Scale out horizontally with Auto Scaling; scaling one instance up hits a ceiling and stays a single point of failure.
API Gateway fronts Lambda or containers with throttling, caching and authorization.
Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows with retries, branching and error handling.
Containers run on ECS or EKS, on Fargate when you do not want to manage servers.
Immutable infrastructure: replace instances from a new AMI or image instead of patching in place.
notes.tip: Sticky sessions tie users to one instance and drop them when it dies. Externalize session state instead.

flowchart LR

  APIGW --> L[Lambda]
  L --> SF[Step Functions workflow]
  SF --> T1[Task: charge card]
  SF --> T2[Task: ship order]
  L --> DDB[(DynamoDB sessions)]

summary.tests: Keeping a workload up when an instance, an AZ or a Region fails, and decoupling tiers so each scales on its own.
must_know: Multi-AZ is for availability; read replicas are for read scaling.
Spread Auto Scaling groups across two or more AZs behind a load balancer.
SQS decouples and buffers; SNS fans out; EventBridge routes events by rules.
FIFO queues give order and exactly-once processing; Standard gives throughput.
DR ladder: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active.
RPO is data loss; RTO is downtime.
Route 53 failover with health checks moves traffic between Regions.
traps: Choosing read replicas when the question asks for automatic failover.
Paying for active-active when the stated RTO allows hours.
A visibility timeout shorter than processing time, which causes duplicate work.

cards.q: RDS must survive an AZ failure with automatic failover. Multi-AZ or read replica?
cards.a: Multi-AZ. Its standby is synchronous and the endpoint fails over automatically. Read replicas are asynchronous and need manual promotion.

cards.q: Reporting queries slow down the production MySQL database. What is the simplest fix?
cards.a: Add an RDS read replica and point the reporting tool at the replica endpoint.

cards.q: How many copies of data does Aurora keep, and where?
cards.a: Six copies across three Availability Zones, on a shared cluster volume.

cards.q: A web tier drops orders when the processing tier is overloaded. What decouples them?
cards.a: An SQS queue between the tiers. Workers poll it and scale on queue depth, so no orders are lost.

cards.q: Messages must be processed exactly once and in order per customer. Which queue type?
cards.a: SQS FIFO, with the customer ID as the message group ID.

cards.q: Messages get processed twice because work takes longer than expected. What do you change?
cards.a: Raise the SQS visibility timeout above the maximum processing time.

cards.q: Where do messages that keep failing go?
cards.a: To a dead-letter queue, after the maxReceiveCount set in the queue's redrive policy.

cards.q: One order event must reach billing, shipping and analytics independently. Which pattern?
cards.a: SNS fan-out to one SQS queue per consumer, or an EventBridge rule per target.

cards.q: Define RPO and RTO.
cards.a: RPO: the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time. RTO: the maximum acceptable time to restore service.

cards.q: DR needs an RTO of minutes, with a scaled-down copy always running. Which strategy?
cards.a: Warm standby. Pilot light keeps only data and core pieces running; active-active runs full capacity.

cards.q: What is the cheapest DR strategy when a day of downtime is acceptable?
cards.a: Backup and restore, for example AWS Backup copying snapshots to another Region.

cards.q: Which Route 53 policy sends users to a standby Region only when the primary health check fails?
cards.a: Failover routing, with a health check on the primary record.

cards.q: How do you point the zone apex example.com at an ALB?
cards.a: A Route 53 alias record. CNAMEs are not allowed at the apex, and alias queries to AWS resources are free.

cards.q: A relational database needs cross-Region reads and DR with about one second of lag. Which service?
cards.a: Aurora Global Database. A secondary Region can be promoted to take writes in about a minute.

cards.q: Lambda functions exhaust RDS connections during traffic spikes. What fixes it?
cards.a: RDS Proxy, which pools and shares database connections and also shortens failover time.

cards.q: Users lose their sessions when an instance in the Auto Scaling group terminates. What is the fix?
cards.a: Store session state outside the instances, in ElastiCache or DynamoDB, so every instance is stateless.

cards.q: A workflow across Lambda functions needs retries, branching and a human approval step. Which service?
cards.a: AWS Step Functions with a Standard workflow, which can wait up to a year.

notes.title: Storage: object, file or block
notes.gist: Match the access type first: objects over HTTP, a block disk for one instance, or a file system shared by many.
points: S3 is object storage: virtually unlimited, eleven nines durability, accessed over HTTP, not a mountable file system.
EBS is block storage for one instance in one AZ; gp3 sets IOPS and throughput apart from size, io2 Block Express gives the most IOPS.
st1 throughput HDD suits big sequential reads, sc1 cold HDD is cheapest; neither can be a boot volume.
EFS is NFS shared by many Linux instances across AZs; FSx for Windows File Server gives SMB and Active Directory.
FSx for Lustre gives HPC throughput linked to S3; instance store is fastest but lost when the instance stops.
Speed up S3 with multipart upload, Transfer Acceleration and parallel requests across prefixes.
notes.tip: Many Linux instances share files: EFS. Windows SMB with Active Directory: FSx for Windows. One database volume needing the most IOPS: io2.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TD
  Q{What kind of access} -->|HTTP objects| S3[(S3)]
  Q -->|one instance, block| EBS[EBS gp3 or io2]
  Q -->|shared Linux NFS| EFS[EFS]
  Q -->|Windows SMB| FSW[FSx for Windows]
  Q -->|HPC scratch| FSL[FSx for Lustre]

notes.title: Elastic compute: right type, right scaling
notes.gist: Choose the instance family or serverless option that fits the job, then scale on the metric that tracks demand.
points: Families: C compute, R and X memory, M general, I storage, G and P GPU, T burstable.
Target tracking holds a metric such as 50 percent CPU; scheduled scaling covers known peaks; predictive scaling learns daily patterns.
Scale worker fleets on SQS backlog per instance, not on CPU.
Lambda runs up to 15 minutes, and its memory setting also sets CPU, so more memory means faster code.
Fargate runs containers without servers; AWS Batch runs queued batch jobs; EMR runs Spark and Hadoop.
Cluster placement groups give the lowest latency for HPC; spread placement groups separate critical instances.
notes.tip: A job that runs longer than 15 minutes is never Lambda. Use Fargate, AWS Batch or EC2.

  POL --> ASG[Auto Scaling group]

notes.title: Databases: pick by access pattern
notes.gist: The data shape and query pattern pick the engine: relational, key-value, warehouse or graph.
points: Relational joins and transactions: RDS or Aurora; Aurora supports up to 15 low-lag read replicas.
Key-value at any scale with single-digit millisecond latency: DynamoDB, in on-demand or provisioned mode.
Analytics warehouse: Redshift. Graph: Neptune. Time series: Timestream. MongoDB-compatible: DocumentDB.
Use Provisioned IOPS storage on RDS when disk I/O is the bottleneck.
Migrate with AWS DMS, adding the Schema Conversion Tool when the engine changes, a heterogeneous migration.
notes.tip: Unpredictable traffic, simple key lookups, no servers: DynamoDB on-demand. Complex SQL reports over terabytes: Redshift, not RDS.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TD

  Q -->|key-value, huge scale| DDB[(DynamoDB)]
  Q -->|analytics, OLAP| RS[(Redshift)]
  Q -->|relationships| NP[(Neptune)]
  DDB --> DAX[DAX microsecond cache]

notes.title: Caching: ElastiCache and DAX
notes.gist: Serve repeated reads from memory so the database only handles misses and writes.
points: Lazy loading fills the cache on a miss: only requested data is cached, but it can be stale.
Write-through updates the cache on every write: always fresh, but it caches data nobody reads.
Add a TTL with either strategy so stale entries expire.
Redis or Valkey: replication, Multi-AZ, persistence, sorted sets for leaderboards. Memcached: simple and multi-threaded, no persistence.
DAX caches DynamoDB reads at microsecond latency through a DynamoDB-compatible client.
Caching helps read-heavy, repetitive workloads; it does little for write-heavy ones.
notes.tip: Repeated identical queries overload the database: ElastiCache in front of RDS. DynamoDB reads need microseconds: DAX.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  APP[App] -->|read| EC[ElastiCache]
  EC -->|hit| APP
  APP -->|miss: query| DB[(RDS)]
  APP -->|store result with TTL| EC

notes.title: Network performance: CloudFront, Global Accelerator, hybrid links
notes.gist: Bring content closer to users with the edge, and pick the load balancer and links that fit the protocol.
points: CloudFront caches HTTP content at edge locations; the origin can be S3 with Origin Access Control, or an ALB.
Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IPs over the AWS backbone for TCP and UDP, with fast Regional failover.
ALB routes HTTP by path and host; NLB handles millions of TCP and UDP requests per second with static IPs.
Transit Gateway connects many VPCs and on-premises networks hub-and-spoke; VPC peering is not transitive.
Direct Connect gives consistent private bandwidth; Site-to-Site VPN is quick to set up over the internet.
notes.tip: Static IPs, UDP gaming or non-HTTP global traffic: Global Accelerator. Cacheable web content: CloudFront.

  U --> GA[Global Accelerator anycast IPs]
  CF --> S3[(S3 origin with OAC)]
  GA --> NLB1[NLB in Region A]
  GA --> NLB2[NLB in Region B]

notes.title: Data ingestion and transformation
notes.gist: Stream data in with Kinesis, land it in S3, catalog it with Glue and query it in place with Athena.
points: Kinesis Data Streams: real time, scales by shards or on-demand, replay for up to 365 days, custom consumers.
Amazon Data Firehose: fully managed delivery to S3, Redshift or OpenSearch, with buffering and optional Lambda transforms.
Glue crawlers build the Data Catalog and Glue jobs run serverless ETL; Athena runs SQL directly on S3.
Store analytics data in S3 as partitioned Parquet so Athena scans less and costs less.
Lake Formation adds fine-grained access control to the data lake; QuickSight builds dashboards.
notes.tip: Load streaming data into S3 with no code or servers: Firehose. Several consumers need real-time reads and replay: Data Streams.

summary.tests: Matching storage, compute, database, caching, network and ingestion services to the stated performance need.
must_know: Object is S3, block is EBS, shared file is EFS or FSx.
gp3 for general SSD, io2 for the most IOPS, st1 and sc1 for cheap sequential HDD.
Target tracking scales on CPU, requests per target or queue backlog.
Lambda runs at most 15 minutes; more memory also means more CPU.
DynamoDB for key-value scale, DAX for microsecond reads, Aurora for relational scale.
ElastiCache for repeated reads: lazy loading versus write-through.
CloudFront caches HTTP; Global Accelerator gives static IPs for TCP and UDP.
Firehose delivers streams to S3; Data Streams for real-time custom consumers.
traps: Picking EBS for storage shared by many instances in different AZs.
Choosing Lambda for a job that runs longer than 15 minutes.
Using CloudFront for UDP or non-HTTP traffic that needs Global Accelerator.

cards.q: Hundreds of Linux instances across AZs must share one POSIX file system. Which service?
cards.a: Amazon EFS. EBS attaches to instances in a single AZ, and S3 is object storage, not a mountable file system.

cards.q: Windows servers need a shared SMB file share joined to Active Directory. Which service?
cards.a: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.

cards.q: Which EBS type suits a large database that needs the highest sustained IOPS?
cards.a: io2 Block Express Provisioned IOPS SSD. gp3 tops out lower, and HDD types cannot handle heavy random I/O.

cards.q: What is the cheapest EBS type for infrequently accessed, sequential cold data?
cards.a: sc1 Cold HDD. It cannot be used as a boot volume.

cards.q: Large uploads to S3 from distant users are slow. Which two features help?
cards.a: Multipart upload for parallel parts, and S3 Transfer Acceleration, which enters the AWS network at the nearest edge location.

cards.q: A batch job takes 40 minutes. Can it run on Lambda?
cards.a: No. Lambda has a 15-minute maximum. Use Fargate, AWS Batch or EC2.

cards.q: How do you make a CPU-bound Lambda function faster?
cards.a: Raise its memory setting. Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory.

cards.q: Worker instances pull jobs from SQS. Which metric should drive Auto Scaling?
cards.a: Backlog per instance: visible messages divided by running instances, held at a target with a target tracking policy.

cards.q: Traffic spikes every weekday at 9 a.m. How do you have capacity ready in time?
cards.a: Scheduled scaling before 9 a.m., or predictive scaling, which learns the daily pattern.

cards.q: HPC nodes need the lowest network latency between instances. Which placement group?
cards.a: A cluster placement group in a single AZ. Spread placement groups put instances on separate hardware instead.

cards.q: DynamoDB reads must drop from milliseconds to microseconds with minimal code change. What do you add?
cards.a: DynamoDB Accelerator DAX, an in-memory cache that uses the DynamoDB API.

cards.q: Lazy loading or write-through: which keeps the cache always current?
cards.a: Write-through, because every write also updates the cache. Lazy loading can serve stale data until the TTL expires.

cards.q: A leaderboard cache needs replication, persistence and sorted sets. Redis or Memcached?
cards.a: ElastiCache for Redis or Valkey. Memcached has no replication, no persistence and no advanced data types.

cards.q: A global UDP game needs two static IPs and fast Regional failover. Which service?
cards.a: AWS Global Accelerator. CloudFront only serves HTTP and HTTPS.

cards.q: Clickstream data must land in S3 in near real time with no servers or code. Which service?
cards.a: Amazon Data Firehose, formerly Kinesis Data Firehose, with buffering and optional Lambda transforms.

cards.q: Analysts want ad hoc SQL over CSV and Parquet files in S3 with no infrastructure. Which service?
cards.a: Amazon Athena, using the Glue Data Catalog for table definitions.

cards.q: You are moving Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL. Which tools do you use?
cards.a: The AWS Schema Conversion Tool for the schema, then AWS DMS to migrate and replicate the data.

notes.title: EC2 purchasing options
notes.gist: Commit for the steady baseline, use Spot for anything interruptible, and keep On-Demand for the rest.
points: On-Demand: no commitment and the highest rate; for short, unpredictable or new workloads.
Reserved Instances and Savings Plans: a 1 or 3 year commitment for up to 72 percent off steady usage.
Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate and Lambda across families and Regions; EC2 Instance Savings Plans save more but lock one family in one Region.
Spot: up to 90 percent off with a two-minute interruption notice; for stateless, fault-tolerant, flexible jobs.
Dedicated Hosts suit per-socket or per-core licences; On-Demand Capacity Reservations guarantee capacity with no discount.
Mix them: a Savings Plan for the baseline, On-Demand or Spot for the peaks.
notes.tip: Interruptible batch or CI work: Spot. A steady 24/7 baseline for a year or more: Savings Plan or RI. A database that must not be interrupted is never Spot.

notes.title: S3 storage classes and lifecycle rules
notes.gist: Pay less for data you touch less, and let lifecycle rules move or delete it on a schedule.
points: Standard for hot data; Standard-IA and One Zone-IA for infrequent access, with a retrieval fee and a 30-day minimum.
One Zone-IA keeps data in a single AZ, so use it only for data you can recreate.
Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between tiers automatically for unknown or changing access, for a small monitoring fee and no retrieval fees.
Glacier Instant Retrieval returns data in milliseconds, Flexible Retrieval in minutes to hours, Deep Archive within 12 to 48 hours at the lowest price.
Lifecycle rules transition objects by age and expire old versions and incomplete multipart uploads.
Requester Pays makes the downloader pay for requests and data transfer.
notes.tip: Unknown access pattern: Intelligent-Tiering. Read once a quarter but needed instantly: Glacier Instant Retrieval. Kept seven years and rarely read: Deep Archive.

notes.title: Block, file and hybrid storage cost
notes.gist: Right-size volumes, tier cold files, and choose the cheapest way to move data in.
points: gp3 costs up to 20 percent less per GB than gp2 and lets you buy IOPS without buying size.
EFS lifecycle management moves cold files to Infrequent Access or Archive automatically.
DataSync copies large datasets online from NFS or SMB to S3, EFS or FSx, on a schedule, with integrity checks.
Snowball Edge ships tens of terabytes or more when the network would take weeks.
Storage Gateway File Gateway lets on-premises apps keep NFS or SMB while data lands in S3; Tape Gateway replaces backup tapes.
Transfer Family gives managed SFTP into S3 or EFS for partners.
notes.tip: 100 TB over a slow link with a deadline: Snowball. Ongoing online sync: DataSync. Apps must keep using a local file share: Storage Gateway.

notes.title: Network and data transfer cost
notes.gist: Data in is free, data out and across AZs is not; keep traffic private, local and cached.
points: Data into AWS is free; data out to the internet is charged; traffic between AZs is charged in each direction.
Traffic within one AZ over private IPs is free; traffic between Regions is charged.
NAT gateways bill per hour and per GB processed; send S3 and DynamoDB traffic through free gateway endpoints instead.
CloudFront egress is cheaper than serving straight from S3 or EC2, and caching cuts origin load too.
Direct Connect lowers the per-GB rate for large, steady on-premises transfer; VPN is cheaper to start.
notes.tip: High NAT gateway bill from S3 traffic: add an S3 gateway endpoint. Cheapest global delivery of static files: CloudFront in front of S3.

notes.title: Cost-effective compute, databases and cost tools
notes.gist: Right-size first, prefer pay-per-use for spiky loads, and watch spend with tags, Cost Explorer and Budgets.
points: Right-size with Compute Optimizer before buying commitments; Graviton instances give better price performance.
Lambda and Fargate bill per use and suit spiky or mostly idle loads; steady high load is often cheaper on EC2.
Aurora Serverless v2 and DynamoDB on-demand suit unpredictable load; provisioned capacity with auto scaling suits steady load.
Stop dev instances out of hours with a schedule; EC2 hibernation keeps memory for fast restarts.
Cost Explorer shows trends and forecasts, Budgets alerts on thresholds, the Cost and Usage Report gives line-item detail.
Cost allocation tags split spend by team or project; consolidated billing pools volume discounts.
notes.tip: Alert when spend will pass a limit: AWS Budgets. Analyse past cost by service or tag: Cost Explorer. Most detailed data for Athena: the CUR.

summary.tests: Choosing the cheapest option that still meets the requirement across compute, storage, databases and the network.
must_know: Spot for interruptible work; Savings Plans or RIs for a steady baseline.
Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate and Lambda flexibly.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering for unknown access; lifecycle rules for known ageing.
Glacier Deep Archive is cheapest for long retention, with 12 to 48 hour retrieval.
gp3 is cheaper than gp2; sc1 is the cheapest HDD.
Gateway endpoints remove NAT data processing charges for S3 and DynamoDB.
Budgets alerts, Cost Explorer analyses, the CUR gives line items.
traps: Using Spot for a database or a job that cannot be interrupted.
Choosing One Zone-IA for data that cannot be recreated.
Forgetting retrieval fees and minimum storage durations on IA and Glacier classes.

cards.q: A nightly batch job can restart if interrupted. What is the cheapest EC2 option?
cards.a: Spot Instances: up to 90 percent off On-Demand, with a two-minute interruption notice.

cards.q: A fleet runs 24/7 for three years but may change instance families and move to Fargate. Which commitment?
cards.a: A Compute Savings Plan. It applies across instance families, Regions, Fargate and Lambda.

cards.q: What does an EC2 Instance Savings Plan give up for its deeper discount?
cards.a: Flexibility: it is tied to one instance family in one Region, though size, OS and tenancy can change.

cards.q: Software is licensed per physical core. Which EC2 option fits?
cards.a: Dedicated Hosts, which expose sockets and cores for bring-your-own-licence.

cards.q: Objects have unpredictable access patterns. Which S3 class lowers cost automatically?
cards.a: S3 Intelligent-Tiering. It moves objects between tiers with no retrieval fees, for a small per-object monitoring charge.

cards.q: Compliance archives must be kept ten years and are almost never read. Which S3 class is cheapest?
cards.a: S3 Glacier Deep Archive, with standard retrieval within 12 hours and bulk retrieval within 48.

cards.q: Data is rarely read but must come back in milliseconds when needed. Which S3 class?
cards.a: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, or Standard-IA if it is read about once a month.

cards.q: When is S3 One Zone-IA acceptable?
cards.a: Only for infrequently accessed data you can recreate, such as thumbnails or secondary copies. It is lost if the AZ is destroyed.

cards.q: Logs should move to cheaper storage after 30 days and be deleted after a year. How?
cards.a: An S3 Lifecycle rule with a transition action at 30 days and an expiration action at 365 days.

cards.q: Partners download a large dataset from your bucket. How do you stop paying for their downloads?
cards.a: Turn on Requester Pays so the downloader's account pays for requests and data transfer.

cards.q: Which EBS change usually cuts cost with no loss of performance?
cards.a: Move gp2 volumes to gp3: up to 20 percent cheaper per GB, with a 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s baseline at any size.

cards.q: 80 TB must reach S3 within a week over a 100 Mbps link. What do you use?
cards.a: AWS Snowball Edge. The link would need more than two months; Snowball ships the data physically.

cards.q: The NAT gateway bill is high because private instances pull large files from S3. What is the fix?
cards.a: Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint. It has no hourly or per-GB charge, so S3 traffic bypasses the NAT gateway.

cards.q: Which costs more: traffic between two AZs, or traffic within one AZ on private IPs?
cards.a: Between AZs, charged in each direction. Same-AZ traffic over private IP addresses is free.

cards.q: You need an email alert when forecast monthly spend will exceed 1,000 USD. Which tool?
cards.a: AWS Budgets with a forecasted cost alert. Cost Explorer analyses spend but does not send alerts.

cards.q: A relational database is idle most of the day with sudden unpredictable bursts. Which option is cost-effective?
cards.a: Aurora Serverless v2, which scales capacity in small steps and bills per ACU-second.

cards.q: Which service recommends right-sized EC2 instance types from utilization data?
cards.a: AWS Compute Optimizer. Trusted Advisor also flags idle and underused resources.
